To defray means to pay for a cost or expense, or to provide money that covers it — either fully or partially.

When you defray an expense, you are essentially absorbing or bearing a financial burden. Think of it as stepping up and saying: "I'll take care of this cost."

You might wonder: why not just say "pay"? The difference is subtle but real.

  • "Pay" is general — you pay for a meal, pay a friend, pay a bill.
  • "Defray" is specifically about covering a cost that exists as a burden — often a significant one, and often on behalf of someone else or for a specific purpose. It carries the idea of relieving a financial pressure.

Think of it this way: you pay for your coffee. But a scholarship defrays your tuition fees. The word carries a slightly more formal, purposeful weight.
What "Defray" Is Almost Always Used With

This is important. "Defray" is almost never used alone. It is nearly always followed by words like:

  • defray the costs
  • defray the expenses
  • defray the charges
  • defray the fees

You will almost never hear someone say "defray a sandwich" or "defray a gift." The word lives specifically in the world of costs, expenses, and financial burdens.

Also very common is the phrase "help defray", which signals that the payment is partial — it reduces the burden without necessarily eliminating it entirely.
The Register: When Do People Use This Word?

"Defray" is a formal word. You will encounter it most often in:

  • Official documents (government policies, legal contracts)
  • Business and finance writing
  • Academic or institutional contexts (grants, scholarships, research funding)
  • Formal journalism

You would rarely hear it in casual everyday conversation. Nobody at a restaurant says "I'll defray your burger." But you absolutely would read: "The organization offered a grant to defray research expenses."
Examples That Show It in Action

Read these carefully — the examples do a lot of the teaching:

  1. "The company agreed to defray all travel expenses for its employees attending the conference."

(The company will cover/pay for the travel costs.)

  1. "They organized a charity auction to help defray the cost of her cancer treatment."

(The auction would partially cover the medical costs — note "help defray" signals it may not cover everything.)

  1. "The government introduced a subsidy to defray the rising cost of fuel for low-income households."

(The government provided money to absorb part of the fuel cost burden.)

  1. "A generous donor offered to defray the expenses of renovating the community library."

(The donor offered to pay for the renovation costs.)

  1. "Students can apply for financial aid to help defray their tuition fees."

(Financial aid reduces the burden of tuition fees.)
The Most Important Things to Lock In

Here is a clean summary of everything that makes "defray" exactly what it is:

  • It means to pay for or cover a cost/expense.
  • It often implies that the cost is significant or burdensome.
  • It frequently (though not always) involves one party covering costs for another — or a fund/resource absorbing an expense.
  • It can mean full or partial coverage of a cost ("help defray" leans toward partial).
  • It is a formal word, paired almost exclusively with words like costs, expenses, charges, and fees.
  • It is about relieving a financial burden, not just making a routine payment.
One Final Way to Remember It

Picture someone struggling to carry a very heavy financial load — a pile of bills and expenses. To defray is to walk up and take some or all of that weight off their hands. The word always lives in that space: a burden, a cost, and someone stepping in to cover it.
